title: The default is a decision.
dek: Germany asks people to opt in as organ donors and 12% do. Austria asks them to opt out and 99.98% stay in. Most of my day is decided the same way, by whatever happens if I do nothing.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile din backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole deja publicate, așa că am adăugat una nouă: default-urile (Austria vs Germania la donarea de organe, 99,98% vs 12%), legată de faptul că azi e sâmbătă, ziua fără orar. entry.title: The default is a decision.
entry.dek: Germany asks people to opt in as organ donors and 12% do. Austria asks them to opt out and 99.98% stay in. Most of my day is decided the same way, by whatever happens if I do nothing.
body: “If you do not choose, somebody already chose for you.”

Have you ever asked yourself how many of the things you did today you actually decided to do? Today is Saturday, the 21st of November, and Saturday is the day with no timetable. Nobody tells me when to wake up, what to study or when to stop. So it should be the day where everything I do is my choice. And yet, when I look back at most Saturdays, I did not choose much - I just did whatever was already there. The question is: if nobody decides for you, who decides? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is called a default. A default is what happens when you do nothing. The settings a new phone comes with, the next episode that starts by itself, the plate that is already full when it reaches the table. I met the word properly in a study about organ donors, and it changed how I look at my own day, because I realised that most of my day is made of defaults that I never picked.

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “The default” and “is a decision”. The first half sounds like nothing - it is literally the option for people who did not decide. The second half is the uncomfortable part. Somebody had to decide what happens when you do nothing. A company, a school, a government, or the version of you from last week who left the phone on the desk and the book in the bag. <u>Doing nothing is never neutral, it is just agreeing with whoever set the default.</u>

Secondly, let’s look at the numbers, because this is where it surprised me. Germany and Austria are neighbours, they speak the same language and they are not very different countries. But they ask about organ donation in opposite ways. In Germany you are not a donor unless you sign up. In Austria you are a donor unless you say no. Two researchers, Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein, put the two side by side:
Germany, where you have to opt in: 12% are donors
Austria, where you have to opt out: 99.98% are donors
That is a difference of almost 88 points, and Austria has about 8 times more donors - for two neighbours answering the same question. The only thing that changed was what happens if you do nothing.

And it is not only about organs. In 2001, Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied an American company that changed its retirement savings plan. Before, new employees had to sign up if they wanted to save. After, they were signed up automatically and had to fill in a form if they did not want it. Among the new employees, participation went from 37% to 86%. Same salaries, same company, same plan, more than double the people saving. The title of their paper says everything: “The Power of Suggestion”.

Now let’s bring it to my own week, because that is the part that I can actually change. These numbers are my assumptions, not a measurement. Let’s say that in the evening my default is the phone, and on 1 day out of 4 I am strong enough to put it away and read instead. Now let’s say that I flip the default - the book is already open on the desk and the phone is charging in another room - and on 1 day out of 4 I am weak and go and get the phone anyway. Over 4 weeks:
Default is the phone: 28 × 1/4 = 7 evenings of reading
Default is the book: 28 × 3/4 = 21 evenings of reading
Same person, same willpower, the same 1 day out of 4 where I go against the default. And the result is 3 times bigger. Willpower decides the exceptions. The default decides everything else.

This is also why I think “just try harder” is such bad advice for most things. Trying harder only works on the days you are going against the default, and those are the minority by definition. If I need to win a fight with myself every evening to do the thing I want, I will lose most of the fights, not because I am weak but because there are a lot of them. Changing the default is one fight, and then it keeps working on the days I do not have the energy to fight at all.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. A default is powerful in both directions, and somebody else is very often the one who picks it. In the same retirement study, many of the new employees did not only stay in the plan, they also stayed at the savings rate and the investment the company had picked for them, which were very careful choices, not necessarily the right ones for a 25 year old. So the default got them in, and then the same laziness kept many of them saving less than they probably would have chosen. <u>A good default can still be a bad final answer.</u> And the apps on my phone have defaults too - the autoplay, the notifications, the endless feed - and those were not chosen with my evening in mind.

So here is what I am going to do today, because it is Saturday and there is no timetable to blame. I am going to look at my room and my phone and ask one question about each thing: what happens if I do nothing? The book goes on the desk, open. The phone charges by the door, not by the bed. The notifications that I never once asked for get turned off. None of this needs motivation tomorrow, it only needs ten minutes today.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most of what I call my habits are just defaults I never questioned, and that changing a default is the cheapest thing I can do for myself. But I have to be honest about two things. Setting your own defaults is still only a guess - I might put the book on the desk and discover that I simply do not want to read it, and then the problem was never the phone. And there is something a little bit sad about tricking myself, as if I cannot be trusted to choose. Maybe the goal is not to live by better defaults forever, but to need them less with time.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“If you do not choose, somebody already chose for you.”
